prompt: What problem were Fischer projections, proposed by Emil Fischer in 1891, meant to solve?

choices.text: Carbohydrates have many chirality centers, so a quick way to show their stereochemistry was needed
Carbohydrates have no chirality centers, so their stereochemistry was hard to see
choices.why: It is the reverse: most carbohydrates have numerous chirality centers.

choices.text: Chemists needed a way to show the true three-dimensional conformation of a sugar
choices.why: Fischer projections don't give an accurate picture of the true conformation, which is curled around like a bracelet.

choices.text: Chemists needed a way to draw the mechanisms of sugar reactions with curved arrows
choices.why: Fischer projections represent the stereochemistry at chirality centers, not reaction mechanisms.

explanation: Because most carbohydrates have numerous chirality centers, a quick method for representing their stereochemistry was needed. In 1891, Emil Fischer suggested projecting a tetrahedral carbon onto a flat surface, and Fischer projections are still a common way to show carbohydrate stereochemistry.

prompt: In a Fischer projection, a tetrahedral carbon is drawn as two crossed lines. What do the horizontal lines represent?

choices.text: Bonds coming out of the page, toward the viewer
Bonds going into the page, away from the viewer
choices.why: That is what the vertical lines represent.

choices.text: Bonds lying flat in the plane of the page
choices.why: None of the four bonds lies in the page: horizontal bonds come out of it and vertical bonds go into it.

choices.text: Double bonds to the central carbon
choices.why: The crossed lines stand for the four single bonds of a tetrahedral carbon.

explanation: A tetrahedral carbon atom is represented in a Fischer projection by two crossed lines. The horizontal lines represent bonds coming out of the page, and the vertical lines represent bonds going into the page.

prompt: How many kinds of motion of a Fischer projection on the paper keep its meaning unchanged?
explanation: Only two kinds of motions are allowed: rotating the projection 180° on the page, and holding one group steady while rotating the other three clockwise or counterclockwise. Moving a Fischer projection in any other way inverts its meaning.

prompt: Which rotation of a Fischer projection on the page keeps it representing the same molecule?

choices.why: A 90° rotation exchanges the groups that go into the plane with those that come out, so it represents the enantiomer.
Like a 90° turn, a 270° turn breaks the Fischer convention. Only a 180° rotation is allowed.

choices.text: Any rotation, as long as the drawing stays in the plane of the page
choices.why: Only a 180° rotation keeps the same groups going into and coming out of the plane.

explanation: A Fischer projection can be rotated on the page by 180°, but not by 90° or 270°. Only a 180° rotation maintains the Fischer convention by keeping the same substituent groups going into and coming out of the plane.

prompt: A Fischer projection of (R)-glyceraldehyde is rotated 90° on the page. What does the rotated projection represent?

choices.text: (S)-glyceraldehyde
(R)-glyceraldehyde, since the molecule itself hasn't changed
choices.why: A 90° turn breaks the Fischer convention, so the new drawing no longer stands for the same molecule. That works only for 180°.

choices.text: A diastereomer of (R)-glyceraldehyde
choices.why: Glyceraldehyde has a single chirality center, so the only other stereoisomer is its enantiomer.

choices.text: Nothing meaningful, because a turned projection can't be read
choices.why: The rotated drawing is still a valid Fischer projection; it simply represents the other enantiomer.

explanation: In (R)-glyceraldehyde the –H and –OH groups come out of the plane. After a 90° rotation they go into the plane, so the rotated projection represents (S)-glyceraldehyde.

prompt: Why does a 90° rotation change the meaning of a Fischer projection?

choices.text: It swaps the groups pointing into the plane with those pointing out
It changes the priority ranking of the four groups around the carbon
choices.why: Rankings depend on the atoms in each group, not on where the group is drawn.

choices.text: It requires breaking one of the bonds at the chirality center
choices.why: No bond is broken; the drawing is only turned on the page.

choices.text: It moves the carbonyl group away from its place at the top
choices.why: A 180° rotation also moves the top group to the bottom, yet keeps the meaning. What matters is which groups point in and which point out.

explanation: Horizontal lines mean bonds toward the viewer and vertical lines mean bonds away. A 90° rotation turns horizontal bonds into vertical ones, exchanging the groups that go into the plane with those that come out, so the projection now shows the enantiomer.

prompt: In a Fischer projection of (R)-glyceraldehyde, the –H and –OH groups are on the horizontal bonds. Where do they point after the projection is rotated 180° on the page?

choices.text: Still out of the plane, toward the viewer
Into the plane, away from the viewer
choices.why: That happens after a 90° rotation, which is why a 90° turn isn't allowed.

choices.text: One into the plane and one out of it
choices.why: Both stay on horizontal bonds after a 180° turn, so both still point out of the plane.

choices.text: Flat in the plane of the page
choices.why: No bond in a Fischer projection lies in the page; horizontal bonds come out of it.

explanation: After a 180° rotation the –H and –OH groups of (R)-glyceraldehyde still come out of the plane, just as before. That is why a 180° rotation keeps the Fischer convention and the R configuration.

prompt: What is the effect of holding one group of a Fischer projection steady while rotating the other three groups clockwise or counterclockwise?

choices.text: Nothing changes; it is simply a rotation around a single bond
The projection now represents the enantiomer of the original
choices.why: This is one of the two allowed motions; it doesn't change the stereochemistry.

choices.text: It keeps the stereochemistry only if the group held steady is –H
choices.why: Any group can be held steady. In Worked Example 25.2.1, –CH3 is held steady.

choices.text: It keeps the stereochemistry only if the three groups turn clockwise
choices.why: The other three groups can be rotated in either a clockwise or a counterclockwise direction.

explanation: A Fischer projection can have one group held steady while the other three rotate in either a clockwise or a counterclockwise direction. The effect is simply to rotate around a single bond, which does not change the stereochemistry.

prompt: When assigning R or S to a Fischer projection, why do you first use an allowed motion to put the lowest-ranked group at the top?

choices.text: A top bond points away from the viewer, as R,S assignment requires
The lowest-ranked group must point toward the viewer, and top bonds do
choices.why: Top (vertical) bonds point away from the viewer, and that is where the lowest-ranked group must point for R,S assignment.

choices.text: That way the highest-ranked group ends up at the bottom, where it must be
choices.why: Only the lowest-ranked group has to be placed; then you read the direction 1 → 2 → 3 of the other three.

choices.text: Groups at the top of a Fischer projection are ignored when ranking
choices.why: All four groups are ranked first, in the usual way, before any group is moved.

explanation: Step 2 places the group of lowest ranking, usually H, at the top of the Fischer projection by an allowed motion. Vertical bonds go into the page, so the lowest-ranked group is then oriented back, away from the viewer. Step 3 reads the direction 1 → 2 → 3 of the other groups.

prompt: In Worked Example 25.2.1, how are the four groups on the chirality center of alanine ranked, from highest to lowest?

choices.text: –NH2 > –CO2H > –CH3 > –H
–CO2H > –NH2 > –CH3 > –H
choices.why: Nitrogen has a higher atomic number than carbon, so –NH2 ranks first.

choices.text: –NH2 > –CH3 > –CO2H > –H
choices.why: The carbon of –CO2H carries oxygen atoms, so it outranks the carbon of –CH3, which carries only hydrogens.

choices.text: –CO2H > –CH3 > –NH2 > –H
choices.why: The atom attached to the chirality center is compared first: N beats C, so –NH2 is first.

explanation: The rankings are (1) –NH2, (2) –CO2H, (3) –CH3, and (4) –H. Nitrogen outranks carbon, and the carboxyl carbon, bonded to oxygens, outranks the methyl carbon.

prompt: A Fischer projection of alanine has –CO2H at the top, –CH3 at the bottom, –NH2 on the left, and –H on the right. What is its configuration?

choices.text: S
R
choices.why: Bring –H to the top first: hold –CH3 steady and rotate the other three counterclockwise. Then –NH2 → –CO2H → –CH3 runs counterclockwise, which is S.

choices.text: It can't be assigned unless the projection is first rotated 90° to put –H on top
choices.why: A 90° rotation isn't allowed; it would turn the projection into its enantiomer. Holding one group steady and rotating the others moves –H instead.

choices.text: It has no chirality center
choices.why: The central carbon carries four different groups (–NH2, –CO2H, –CH3, –H), so it is a chirality center.

explanation: This is Worked Example 25.2.1. Ranking: –NH2 > –CO2H > –CH3 > –H. Holding –CH3 steady and rotating the other three groups counterclockwise puts –H at the top, with –CO2H on the left and –NH2 on the right. Going from –NH2 to –CO2H to –CH3 is then a counterclockwise turn, so the configuration is S.

prompt: A Fischer projection has –CHO at the top, –CH3 at the bottom, –OH on the right, and –H on the left. What is the configuration of its chirality center?

choices.text: R
S, because –OH → –CHO → –CH3 runs counterclockwise as drawn
choices.why: As drawn, –H is on a horizontal bond pointing toward you. Move –H to the top first; then the direction is clockwise, which is R.

choices.text: It can't be assigned unless the projection is first rotated 90° to put –H on top
choices.why: A 90° rotation isn't allowed; it would turn the projection into its enantiomer. Hold one group steady and rotate the other three instead.

choices.text: It has no chirality center
choices.why: The carbon carries four different groups (–OH, –CHO, –CH3, –H), so it is a chirality center.

explanation: Rank the groups: –OH > –CHO > –CH3 > –H. Hold –CH3 steady and rotate the other three clockwise, which puts –H at the top, –CHO on the right, and –OH on the left. Then –OH → –CHO → –CH3 runs clockwise, so the configuration is R (Exercise 25.2.1b).

prompt: A Fischer projection has –CH3 at the top, –CH2CH3 at the bottom, –CHO on the right, and –H on the left. What is the configuration of its chirality center?

choices.text: S
R, because –CHO → –CH2CH3 → –CH3 runs clockwise as drawn
choices.why: As drawn, –H is on a horizontal bond pointing toward you. After an allowed motion puts –H at the top, the direction is counterclockwise: S.

choices.text: R, because –CH2CH3 outranks –CHO
choices.why: The –CHO carbon carries (O, O, H) and outranks the –CH2CH3 carbon, which carries (C, H, H).

choices.text: It has no chirality center, because two of its groups are alkyl groups
choices.why: –CH3 and –CH2CH3 are different groups, so all four groups are different.

explanation: Rank: –CHO > –CH2CH3 > –CH3 > –H. Hold –CH2CH3 steady and rotate the other three clockwise, putting –H at the top, –CH3 on the right, and –CHO on the left. Then –CHO → –CH2CH3 → –CH3 runs counterclockwise, so the configuration is S (Exercise 25.2.1c).

prompt: A Fischer projection of 2-chloro-1-propanol, CH3CHClCH2OH, has –H at the top, –Cl at the bottom, –CH2OH on the left, and –CH3 on the right. What is the configuration of its chirality center?

choices.text: R
S, because the direction must be reversed when –H is at the top
choices.why: No reversal is needed: a top (vertical) bond points away from the viewer, which is exactly what R,S assignment requires.

choices.text: S, because –CH2OH outranks –Cl
choices.why: Chlorine has a higher atomic number than carbon, so –Cl ranks first.

choices.text: It has no chirality center
choices.why: The carbon carries four different groups (–Cl, –CH2OH, –CH3, –H), so it is a chirality center.

explanation: Rank: –Cl > –CH2OH > –CH3 > –H. The lowest-ranked group, –H, is already at the top, pointing back. Going –Cl (bottom) → –CH2OH (left) → –CH3 (right) is a clockwise turn, so the configuration is R. This is the Fischer projection in the answer to Exercise 25.2.3.

prompt: How many chirality centers are stacked on top of one another in a Fischer projection of glucose?
explanation: Carbohydrates with more than one chirality center are shown in Fischer projections by stacking the centers on top of one another. Glucose has four chirality centers stacked this way, with the carbonyl carbon at the top.

prompt: How is a carbohydrate with several chirality centers shown in a Fischer projection?

choices.text: Centers stacked vertically, with the carbonyl carbon at or near the top
Centers side by side, with the carbonyl carbon at the far left
choices.why: The centers are stacked vertically, not drawn side by side.

choices.text: Centers stacked vertically, with the carbonyl carbon at the bottom
choices.why: By convention the carbonyl carbon goes at or near the top.

choices.text: A separate projection for each center, drawn one beside another
choices.why: All the centers appear in a single projection, stacked on top of one another.

explanation: Carbohydrates with more than one chirality center are shown in Fischer projections by stacking the centers on top of one another, with the carbonyl carbon at or near the top.

prompt: What does a Fischer projection of glucose NOT show accurately?

choices.text: Its true three-dimensional shape, curled like a bracelet
The configuration at each of its four chirality centers
choices.why: Showing the stereochemistry at each chirality center is exactly what Fischer projections do.

choices.text: Which of its carbons is the carbonyl (aldehyde) carbon
choices.why: The carbonyl carbon is drawn at or near the top, so it is clear.

choices.text: How many chirality centers the molecule contains
choices.why: All four of glucose's chirality centers are shown, stacked on top of one another.

explanation: Fischer projections show the stereochemistry at each chirality center, but they don't give an accurate picture of the molecule's true three-dimensional conformation, which is curled around on itself like a bracelet.

prompt: A Fischer projection of (R)-glyceraldehyde is rotated 90° on the page and then another 90° in the same direction. What does the final projection represent?

choices.text: (R)-glyceraldehyde
(S)-glyceraldehyde
choices.why: Two 90° turns in the same direction add up to a 180° rotation, which is allowed and keeps the meaning.

choices.text: A 1 : 1 mixture of (R)- and (S)-glyceraldehyde
choices.why: A projection stands for one molecule, not a mixture.

choices.text: A diastereomer of (R)-glyceraldehyde
choices.why: Glyceraldehyde has only one chirality center, so it has no diastereomers. The overall 180° rotation leaves it unchanged.

explanation: Two 90° turns in the same direction are a 180° rotation in total. A 180° rotation keeps the same groups going into and coming out of the plane, so the projection still represents (R)-glyceraldehyde.

prompt: A Fischer projection of glyceraldehyde has –CHO at the top, –CH2OH at the bottom, –OH on the left, and –H on the right. Which of these Fischer projections represents the same enantiomer?

choices.text: –H at the top, –CHO at the bottom, –OH on the left, –CH2OH on the right
–CHO at the top, –CH2OH at the bottom, –OH on the right, –H on the left
choices.why: Exchanging the two horizontal groups gives the mirror image. With –H moved to the top, –OH → –CHO → –CH2OH runs clockwise: this is the R enantiomer.

choices.text: –CH2OH at the top, –CHO at the bottom, –OH on the left, –H on the right
choices.why: Exchanging only the top and bottom groups isn't an allowed motion. Moving –H to the top shows –OH → –CHO → –CH2OH running clockwise: R.

choices.text: –CH2OH at the top, –OH at the bottom, –CHO on the right, –H on the left
choices.why: Moving –H to the top (hold –OH steady, rotate the others clockwise) shows –OH → –CHO → –CH2OH running clockwise: R.

explanation: The starting projection is (S)-glyceraldehyde. Holding its –OH steady and rotating the other three groups counterclockwise gives –H at the top, –CHO at the bottom, and –CH2OH on the right, an allowed motion, so this is the same enantiomer. With –H at the top, –OH → –CHO → –CH2OH runs counterclockwise: S (Exercise 25.2.2).

prompt: In Worked Example 25.2.1, how is –H brought to the top of alanine's Fischer projection (–CO2H top, –CH3 bottom, –NH2 left, –H right)?

choices.text: By holding –CH3 steady and turning the other three counterclockwise
By rotating the whole projection 90° counterclockwise on the page
choices.why: A 90° rotation isn't allowed; it would turn the projection into its enantiomer.

choices.text: By rotating the whole projection 180° so that –H changes sides
choices.why: A 180° rotation is allowed, but it moves –H from the right to the left, not to the top.

choices.text: By exchanging the positions of the –H and –CO2H groups directly
choices.why: Exchanging two groups is not one of the two allowed motions, so it would change the meaning of the projection.

explanation: The worked example holds the –CH3 group steady while rotating the other three groups counterclockwise. That is an allowed motion (a rotation around a single bond), so –H reaches the top without any change in stereochemistry.
